汪來〔貫直隸天津衛軍籍，直隸寧國縣人，國子生，治書經，字伯陽，行一，年二十七，四月二十一日生〕。曾祖禮，祖瀛，父宦，母張氏。具慶下，弟耒，娶王氏。順天府鄉試第一百十八名，會試第一百二十七名。

段鍊〔貫順天府固安縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字文純，行一，年三十，十一月十二日生〕。曾祖紀，祖裕之，父進〔訓導〕，前母王氏，母陶氏。具慶下，兄錦、錄、鏞〔生員〕、鉞，弟鎧、錞，娶王氏。順天府鄉試第六十三名，會試第一百五十一名。

徐貢元〔貫直隸太平府繁昌縣民籍，國子生，治書經，字孔賜，行十九，年三十五，閏正月二十四日生〕。曾祖俊，祖瑞〔義官〕，父昆〔訓導〕，母丁氏。具慶下，弟贊元、賀元、貞元、實元、質元、賢元，娶汪氏。應天府鄉試第一百三名，會試第二百十一名。
translation_en:
He Qian, registered in an official household of the De’an Defense Battalion in Huguang, was a student of the Directorate of Education who specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Maoyi; he ranked first in family birth order and was forty-one years old, born on the fifth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather Hong and grandfather Tai were both Vice Battalion Commanders; his father Xun was a Vice Commander. His mother was née Zhang, and his stepmother née Zhu. Both parents were deceased. His younger brother was Yuan, and his wife was née Yang. He placed thirty-fifth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 134th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Lai, registered in a military household of the Tianjin Guard in Zhili and a native of Ningguo County in Zhili, was a student of the Directorate of Education who specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Boyang; he ranked first in family birth order and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-first day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Li, his grandfather Ying, and his father Huan; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Lai 耒, and his wife was née Wang. He placed 118th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 127th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Duan Lian, registered in a civilian household of Gu’an County, Shuntian Prefecture, was a student of the Directorate of Education who specialized in the Book of Poetry. His courtesy name was Wenchun; he ranked first in family birth order and was thirty years old, born on the twelfth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Ji, his grandfather Yuzhi, and his father Jin, an Assistant Instructor. His father’s former wife was née Wang, and his mother was née Tao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jin, Lu, Yong, a government student, and Yue; his younger brothers were Kai and Chun. His wife was née Wang. He placed sixty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 151st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Gongyuan, registered in a civilian household of Fanchang County, Taiping Prefecture, Zhili, was a student of the Directorate of Education who specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Kongci; he ranked nineteenth in family birth order and was thirty-five years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the intercalary first month. His great-grandfather was Jun, his grandfather Rui, an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions, and his father Kun, an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Ding. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zanyuan, Heyuan, Zhenyuan, Shiyuan, Zhiyuan, and Xianyuan; his wife was née Wang. He placed 103rd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 211th in the Metropolitan Examination.

馬愼，貫順天府霸州大城縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字自脩，行一，年二十六，四月初十日生。曾祖志廣〔贈文林郎〕，祖永〔壽官〕，父齡〔知縣〕，前母孫氏，母郭氏。具慶下，弟恪、惺，娶魏氏。順天府鄉試第四十七名，會試第二百五名。

吳守貞，貫廣東高州府電白縣，軍籍，縣學生，治詩經，字定夫，行四，年三十四，十月初十日生。曾祖政〔歲貢生〕，祖綸〔署教諭舉人〕，父思齊〔縣丞〕，前母劉氏，母陳氏。具慶下，兄守仁、守禮、守忠，弟守謙，娶蕭氏。廣東鄉試第五十一名，會試第一百七十三名。
translation_en:
Ma Shen 馬愼 was registered in Dacheng County, Bazhou, Shuntian Prefecture, in a civilian household. A county-school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Zixiu and ranked first among his brothers. He was twenty-six years old, born on the tenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhiguang〔posthumously awarded the title Gentleman-litterateur〕; his grandfather was Yong〔holder of an honorary official title for longevity〕; and his father was Ling〔County Magistrate〕. His father's former wife was née Sun, and his mother was née Guo. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Ke and Xing, and his wife was née Wei. He placed forty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Shouzhen 吳守貞 was registered in Dianbai County, Gaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, in a military household. A county-school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Dingfu and ranked fourth among his brothers. He was thirty-four years old, born on the tenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zheng〔annual tribute student〕; his grandfather was Lun〔acting County School Instructor and provincial graduate (juren)〕; and his father was Siqi〔Vice Magistrate〕. His father's former wife was née Liu, and his mother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Shouren, Shouli, and Shouzhong; his younger brother was Shouqian. His wife was née Xiao. He placed fifty-first in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 173rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟六經
之道同歸而禮樂
之用為急自昔唐
虞三代之治莫不
由斯夫六經所陳
===
固治天下之大經
大法也而本之則
在禮樂然則政刑
末務果不足以為
治歟抑各適其用

punctuated: 皇帝制曰：「朕惟六經之道同歸，而禮樂之用為急。自昔唐虞三代之治，莫不由斯。夫六經所陳，固治天下之大經大法也，而本之則在禮樂。然則政刑末務，果不足以為治歟？抑各適其用
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “I consider that the teachings of the Six Classics converge upon the same end, yet putting rites and music into practice is most urgent. From antiquity, the governance of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties invariably proceeded from these. What the Six Classics set forth are indeed the great principles and laws for governing all under Heaven, yet their foundation lies in rites and music. Are the subsidiary matters of administration and punishments, then, truly insufficient to achieve good governance? Or does each have its appropriate use …

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
而不能相通歟議
者謂三代而上治
出於一而禮樂達
于天下後世則否
然歟否歟朕纘承
===
皇祖大統
列聖鴻緒踐祚以来
不遑他務首以人
倫典禮是究是圖
盖勤心宵旰者十
alt_text:
而不能相通歟議
者謂三代而上治
出於一而禮樂達
于天下後世則否
然歟否歟朕纘承
===
皇祖大統
列聖鴻緒踐阼以來
不遑他務首以人
倫典禮是究是圖
蓋勤心宵旰者十
punctuated: 而不能相通歟？議者謂三代而上，治出於一，而禮樂達于天下，後世則否。然歟？否歟？朕纘承皇祖大統、列聖鴻緒，踐祚以来，不遑他務，首以人倫典禮是究是圖。盖勤心宵旰者十
translation_en: …and cannot function in conjunction with one another? Those who discuss the matter say that in the Three Dynasties and earlier, government proceeded from a single source, and rites and music extended throughout the realm, whereas in later ages this was no longer so. Since ascending the throne, I have had no leisure for other concerns, devoting myself first to investigating and planning for human relationships and ceremonial observances. Indeed, I have labored anxiously, rising before dawn and eating late, for ten…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
臣沈坤
臣對臣聞帝王之經世也有立治之大本有
善治之大法本者何天德在我所以制作之
根柢也法者何王道四達所以經綸之顯設
也本之不立則法不能以自行法之不善則
本亦有所未盡推究而言之本立而法行者
有矣未有無本而善法者也體具而用周者
有矣未有偏體而無用者也本立法善體用
備矣亦未有治功之不成者也知夫此則禮
樂之務中和之極與夫古今之制作治道之
===
汙隆皆可得而言之矣自昔帝王立極經世
皆本之躬行心得之餘措之彌綸參贊之業
是故修于身齊于家用之于鄉黨邦國以大
同于天下盖不獨當時蒙其至治而施諸後
世猶足以俟聖人考之而不謬其不然者則
圖治無本取給于儀文器數之末本與法判
然二道此治之所以不古若也然豈惟無本
且併其法而失之尚何足以與制作之列乎
恭惟
皇帝陛下合天地陽陰之德總明聖述作之能建

punctuated:
臣沈坤。
臣對：臣聞帝王之經世也，有立治之大本，有善治之大法。本者何？天德在我，所以制作之根柢也。法者何？王道四達，所以經綸之顯設也。本之不立，則法不能以自行；法之不善，則本亦有所未盡。推究而言之，本立而法行者有矣，未有無本而善法者也；體具而用周者有矣，未有偏體而無用者也。本立法善，體用備矣，亦未有治功之不成者也。知夫此，則禮樂之務、中和之極，與夫古今之制作、治道之汙隆，皆可得而言之矣。自昔帝王立極經世，皆本之躬行心得之餘，措之彌綸參贊之業。是故修于身，齊于家，用之于鄉黨邦國，以大同于天下。盖不獨當時蒙其至治，而施諸後世，猶足以俟聖人考之而不謬。其不然者，則圖治無本，取給于儀文器數之末，本與法判然二道，此治之所以不古若也。然豈惟無本？且併其法而失之，尚何足以與制作之列乎？
恭惟皇帝陛下合天地陽陰之德，總明聖述作之能，建
translation_en:
Your servant, Shen Kun.
Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings order the world, they possess both a great foundation for establishing government and great methods for governing well. What is this foundation? It is Heaven’s virtue within oneself, the root from which institutions are created. What are these methods? They are the kingly Way extending in all directions, the manifest arrangements through which the world is ordered. If the foundation is not established, the methods cannot operate of themselves; if the methods are not good, the foundation, too, has not been fully realized. Pursuing the matter further, there have been cases in which the foundation was established and the methods put into practice, but never one in which good methods existed without a foundation. There have been cases in which substance was complete and its functioning comprehensive, but never one in which substance was partial and had no functioning [?]. When the foundation is established and the methods are good, substance and functioning are both complete; never, then, has effective government failed to be achieved. Once this is understood, the tasks of rites and music, the highest attainment of equilibrium and harmony, the institutions of antiquity and the present, and the decline and flourishing of government can all be discussed.
From antiquity, emperors and kings, in establishing the supreme standard and ordering the world, have grounded their work in what they attained through personal practice and inward understanding, applying it to the undertaking of comprehensively ordering things and assisting the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth. Thus they cultivated themselves, regulated their households, and applied this to their local communities and states, thereby bringing great concord to all under Heaven. Not only did their contemporaries enjoy their consummate government: when their institutions were transmitted to later generations, they could still await examination by a sage and be found free of error. Those who acted otherwise sought good government without a foundation, relying instead on such peripheral matters as ceremonial forms, implements, and numerical prescriptions. Foundation and methods became two utterly separate paths. This is why their government fell short of antiquity. Yet was it merely that they lacked a foundation? They also lost the methods themselves. How, then, could they deserve a place among the creators of institutions?
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor unites the virtues of Heaven and Earth, yang and yin, and possesses in full the capacities of the enlightened and the sage both to transmit and to create, establishing…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
中和位育之功撫盈成熈洽之運制禮作樂
盡善盡美信乎遠追古帝王之道而無愧近
守我
祖宗之法而加隆者也猶且進臣等于
廷詢以禮樂之務欲何修以比于先王之盛此
誠
陛下望道未見之心也臣草茅迂賤何足以識此
雖然言及之而不言則謂之隱况黎獻帝臣
方齒于萬邦之舉而愚者千慮或冀于一得
之末哉臣敢不掇拾所聞以對嘗惟六經之
===
道同歸而禮樂之用為急故天高地下萬物
散殊而禮制行矣流而不息合同而化而樂
興焉先王觀履之象以制禮是故有取于天
澤之分而截然不易者其體也觀豫之象以
作樂是故有取于順動之義而歡欣無間者
其情也盖天地示人以和序聖人因造化以
成能且聖人之所以自淑其身心者要亦不
出于禮樂之外粤稽諸古唐虞三代若堯舜
禹湯文武之為君既皆以精一執中之傳建
極于上而一時輔理承化之臣又皆夷夔伊

punctuated:
中和位育之功，撫盈成熈洽之運，制禮作樂，盡善盡美，信乎遠追古帝王之道而無愧，近守我祖宗之法而加隆者也。猶且進臣等于廷，詢以禮樂之務，欲何修以比于先王之盛。此誠陛下望道未見之心也。臣草茅迂賤，何足以識此？雖然，言及之而不言，則謂之隱。况黎獻帝臣，方齒于萬邦之舉，而愚者千慮，或冀于一得之末哉！臣敢不掇拾所聞以對？
嘗惟六經之道同歸，而禮樂之用為急。故天高地下，萬物散殊，而禮制行矣；流而不息，合同而化，而樂興焉。先王觀履之象以制禮，是故有取于天澤之分，而截然不易者，其體也；觀豫之象以作樂，是故有取于順動之義，而歡欣無間者，其情也。盖天地示人以和序，聖人因造化以成能。且聖人之所以自淑其身心者，要亦不出于禮樂之外。粤稽諸古，唐虞三代，若堯舜禹湯文武之為君，既皆以精一執中之傳建極于上，而一時輔理承化之臣，又皆夷夔伊
translation_en:
…the achievement of equilibrium and harmony, whereby Heaven and Earth take their proper places and all things are nurtured; presiding over an age of flourishing accomplishment, prosperity, and concord; establishing rites and creating music, perfect in goodness and beauty. Truly, Your Majesty has emulated the Way of the ancient emperors and kings of distant antiquity without falling short, while upholding and further enhancing the institutions of our own imperial ancestors. Yet you have also summoned us, your servants, to court and questioned us concerning rites and music, asking what should be cultivated to match the flourishing achievements of the former kings. This indeed expresses Your Majesty’s resolve to seek the Way as though you had not yet discerned it. Your servant is an obscure, unworldly man of humble standing: how could I adequately comprehend this? Nevertheless, when a subject arises about which one ought to speak, remaining silent is called concealment. Moreover, as a worthy man from among the common people and a servant of the emperor, I now take my place among those recommended from throughout the realm; even a fool, reflecting a thousand times, may hope to arrive at one small insight. How could your servant dare not gather what he has heard and offer it in reply?
I have reflected that the Ways taught by the Six Classics converge upon the same end, but putting rites and music into practice is especially urgent. Heaven is high and Earth low, and the myriad things are dispersed and distinct: thus the ordering institutions of ritual operate. Things flow without ceasing, unite, and undergo transformation: thus music arises. The former kings contemplated the image of the hexagram Treading (Lü) to establish rites. Accordingly, they drew upon the distinction between Heaven above and the marsh below; clear distinctions that remain unaltered constitute the substance of rites. They contemplated the image of the hexagram Enthusiasm (Yu) to create music. Accordingly, they drew upon the meaning of movement in accord with the natural order; joy without estrangement constitutes the feeling of music. Heaven and Earth show humanity harmony and order, and the sages follow the processes of creation and transformation to fulfill their capacities. Moreover, the means by which the sages themselves refine their persons and minds likewise lie, in essence, within rites and music. Examining antiquity—the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties—we find that rulers such as Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu all established the supreme standard above through the transmitted teaching of refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to the Mean. The ministers of their respective times who assisted their governance and carried forward their transforming influence were, moreover, all men such as Yi, Kui, and Yi…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
傅周召之流典司於下其在當時自民生日
用之常以極于際天蟠地之盛蓋治外無道
道外無治雖未嘗明言禮樂于天下而其治
化之隆已四達而不悖矣宋儒歐陽脩所謂
三代而上治出於一而禮樂達于天下者也
斯時也以禮樂為治即所以為政而刑則視
為輔治之法雖以是為末務要非各適其用
而不能相通者矣至於後世享國之久者莫
如漢唐宋夷考其時雖議禮作樂後先相聞
而要其制度之所就則如綿蕞之習房中之
===
歌貞觀之儀七德之舞與夫通禮之名雅樂
之定紛紛制作未能悉舉大率漢高祖唐太
宗宋藝祖以下諸君既非有純王之德主之
于上而一時任事之臣又非皆庶幾禮樂之
賢以承之于下則其治功之所及要亦止於
漢唐宋而已耳歐陽脩所謂三代而下治出
于二而禮樂為虛文者也斯時也政與治既
為二道則禮樂不過為觀美之具而政刑亦
從事于苟且之間豈止于不相為用而已哉

傅、周、召之流，典司於下。其在當時，自民生日用之常，以極于際天蟠地之盛，蓋治外無道，道外無治。雖未嘗明言禮樂于天下，而其治化之隆，已四達而不悖矣。宋儒歐陽脩所謂三代而上，治出於一，而禮樂達于天下者也。斯時也，以禮樂為治，即所以為政，而刑則視為輔治之法。雖以是為末務，要非各適其用而不能相通者矣。
至於後世，享國之久者，莫如漢、唐、宋。夷考其時，雖議禮作樂，後先相聞，而要其制度之所就，則如綿蕞之習、房中之歌、貞觀之儀、七德之舞，與夫通禮之名、雅樂之定，紛紛制作，未能悉舉。大率漢高祖、唐太宗、宋藝祖以下諸君，既非有純王之德主之于上，而一時任事之臣，又非皆庶幾禮樂之賢以承之于下，則其治功之所及，要亦止於漢、唐、宋而已耳。歐陽脩所謂三代而下，治出于二，而禮樂為虛文者也。斯時也，政與治既為二道，則禮樂不過為觀美之具，而政刑亦從事于苟且之間，豈止于不相為用而已哉！
天啓
translation_en:
…men such as Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao administered affairs below. In their time, from the ordinary matters of people’s daily lives to the vast affairs encompassing heaven and earth, there was no Way apart from governance and no governance apart from the Way. Although they never explicitly proclaimed ritual and music to the world, the flourishing influence of their rule already extended in all directions without discord. This was what the Song Confucian Ouyang Xiu described as: “From the Three Dynasties back into antiquity, governance issued from a single source, and ritual and music pervaded all under heaven.” At that time, governing through ritual and music was itself the conduct of administration, while punishments were regarded as a means of assisting governance. Although punishment was treated as a subsidiary concern, these were certainly not separate instruments, each serving its own purpose without connection to the others.
As for later ages, no dynasties endured longer than the Han, Tang, and Song. On examining those times, we find successive reports of deliberations on ritual and the creation of music. Yet, considering what their institutions actually achieved, there were such things as the rehearsal of ceremonies using bundles of reeds as markers, the Songs of the Inner Chambers, the ceremonial regulations of the Zhenguan era, the Dance of the Seven Virtues, the work called Comprehensive Rites, and the establishment of court ceremonial music. Their numerous creations cannot all be enumerated. In general, the rulers from Gaozu of Han, Taizong of Tang, and Yizu of Song onward did not preside above with the virtue of true sage kings, nor were the ministers serving at those times all worthy men who approached mastery of ritual and music and could sustain their rulers below. Thus, the achievements of their governance ultimately reached no further than the level of the Han, Tang, and Song. This was what Ouyang Xiu described as: “After the Three Dynasties, governance issued from two sources, and ritual and music became empty forms.” At that time, administration and the achievement of good order had already become two separate paths. Ritual and music were consequently no more than instruments of outward display, while administration and punishment were pursued through expedient improvisation. How could the problem have been merely that they failed to serve one another’s purposes!
Heaven inaugurated…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
國朝我
太祖高皇帝用夏變夷復綱常於淪斁之後除殘
去暴拯生民于塗炭之中所謂以聖人之德
在天子之位而又當興王之始三重既備則
制作之任自不容逭故於洪武初年天下甫
定雖日不暇給而必首以禮樂爲重徵賢分
局講究切劘方開天肇紀之初其規摸宏遠
已非復漢唐宋之草率矣盖我
太祖以天縱聖神之資得治躬治心之道凡履中
正而樂和平之實備載于
===
聖政記諸書者可考而知也方是時明良契合天
作之會夷夔經濟殆不止于陶凱牛諒諸臣
而已若今
大明集禮一書其旨則斷自
宸衷其成則出于曾魯徐一夔董彝梁寅諸臣之
手其禮之目二十有六以至于冠服車輅儀
仗鹵簿之制其樂之成有九以至于黃鍾太
吕絃歌干羽之式禮樂明備凡以和神人而
諧上下者未必非我
太祖制作之意而在當時諸臣亦足以爲會其成

太祖制作之意而在當時諸臣亦足以爲會其成
punctuated:
國朝我太祖高皇帝用夏變夷，復綱常於淪斁之後，除殘去暴，拯生民于塗炭之中。所謂以聖人之德，在天子之位，而又當興王之始，三重既備，則制作之任自不容逭。故於洪武初年，天下甫定，雖日不暇給，而必首以禮樂爲重，徵賢分局，講究切劘。方開天肇紀之初，其規摸宏遠，已非復漢唐宋之草率矣。盖我太祖以天縱聖神之資，得治躬治心之道，凡履中正而樂和平之實，備載于《聖政記》諸書者，可考而知也。
方是時，明良契合，天作之會，夷夔經濟，殆不止于陶凱、牛諒諸臣而已。若今《大明集禮》一書，其旨則斷自宸衷，其成則出于曾魯、徐一夔、董彝、梁寅諸臣之手。其禮之目二十有六，以至于冠服、車輅、儀仗、鹵簿之制；其樂之成有九，以至于黃鍾、太吕、絃歌、干羽之式。禮樂明備，凡以和神人而諧上下者，未必非我太祖制作之意，而在當時諸臣，亦足以爲會其成
translation_en:
…our dynasty. Our Emperor Taizu Gao transformed the barbarians through the ways of Xia, restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues after their collapse and corruption, eliminated the cruel and violent, and rescued the people from utter misery. He exemplified what is meant by possessing the virtue of a sage while occupying the position of the Son of Heaven, and he also stood at the beginning of a new royal enterprise. With the three weighty prerequisites fulfilled, he could not evade responsibility for establishing rites and institutions. Thus, in the early Hongwu years, when the realm had only just been pacified, although each day scarcely afforded enough time for his duties, he invariably gave priority to ritual and music. He summoned worthy men, assigned them to separate bureaus, and had them investigate, discuss, and refine these matters together. At the very inception of the dynasty, his designs were already so grand and far-reaching that they surpassed the cursory arrangements of the Han, Tang, and Song. For our Taizu, endowed by Heaven with sagely and wondrous qualities, grasped the way to govern his person and his mind. The actual manifestations of his adherence to balance and correctness and his delight in peace and harmony, fully recorded in such books as the Record of Sagely Government (Shengzheng ji), can be examined and understood.
At that time, an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers were joined in accord—a union made by Heaven. Those who ordered the realm in the manner of Boyi and Kui surely included more than such ministers as Tao Kai and Niu Liang alone. Take the extant Compendium of Rituals of the Great Ming (Da Ming jili): its guiding principles were determined by the imperial mind, while its completion was the work of such ministers as Zeng Lu, Xu Yikui, Dong Yi, and Liang Yin. Its ritual categories numbered twenty-six, extending to regulations for caps and robes, carriages, ceremonial insignia, and processional escorts. Its musical movements numbered nine, extending to the forms governing the Huangzhong and Dalu pitch standards, strings and singing, and dances with shields and feathers. Ritual and music were clearly set out and fully provided for. All these means of bringing spirits and humans into harmony and concord to superiors and inferiors may well have embodied our Taizu’s intentions in establishing these institutions; the ministers of that time, too, could be credited with bringing the undertaking to completion…

皇上極建中和功收位育同符

正名之初所謂聖人乘時之會天下改觀易
聽之時也臣在學校嘗伏讀

translation_en:
…indeed. Yet the combined suburban and soil sacrifices were performed together at one time; the winter and autumn offerings in the ancestral temple did not distinguish between separate sacrifices and joint sacrifices to the ancestors; the rites of the great di sacrifice had not been investigated and expounded; and no clear proposal had been advanced concerning the Hall of Light. Since the successive sage emperors inherited and maintained the great enterprise, they have followed these practices: what had been instituted, none dared abolish; what had been abolished, none dared institute. Yet the circumstances of founding and preserving a dynasty differ, as do preferences for refinement and simplicity. Moreover, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors did not all follow the same precedents. Only a sage can fittingly carry on his predecessors’ work and fulfill their intentions. Thus, if today’s rites and music are to develop from broad outlines into detailed forms, adapting to the times while following the Way, how could this not await Your Majesty?
For Your Majesty has established the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony, achieving the proper ordering of Heaven and Earth and the nourishment of all things. You match Taizu and far surpass the rulers of Tang and Yu; both your virtue and your position are exalted. Moreover, you reign more than a hundred years into the dynasty’s course, when the achievements of government are established, at the inception of renewed deliberations concerning succession to the imperial line and the rectification of names in human relationships. This is what is meant by the moment when a sage takes advantage of his time, when all under Heaven see and hear anew. While in school, your servant reverently read the Great Compendium on Clarifying Human Relationships (Minglun dadian), and already understood the care Your Majesty devotes to the cardinal bonds and human relationships. Now, none but a sage can institute rites. Once they have been instituted and their underlying sentiments fully expressed, then whatever leaves his heart uneasy must all…

translation_en:
…cannot be left unchanged. Thereafter, whenever the great rites were revised, an edict invariably announced the changes throughout the realm. Thus, Heaven and Earth were formerly worshipped together. Now, with the establishment of the southern and northern suburban sacrificial grounds, the Circular Mound and the Square Marsh are distinguished as a raised altar and a sunken precinct, each occupying its proper position and direction. The sacrifices were also formerly performed together on the first xin day. Now they are held at the winter and summer solstices, rooted respectively in yin and yang, following their natural order to meet with auspiciousness: the seasons and days must accord with their respective categories.
At the beginning of the dynasty, four temples for the immediate ancestors were first established. Subsequently, the Imperial Ancestral Temples in the two capitals adopted a common hall with separate chambers. His Majesty has specially established an Imperial Ancestral Temple to offer worship to Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, in recompense for his achievement in founding the dynasty. He has founded a temple to Chengzu, whose tablet will remain unmoved for a hundred generations, to exalt Emperor Wen’s virtue in preserving the inherited achievement. From Renzong and Xuanzong onward, the three zhao and three mu ancestors each have a separate temple; when the prescribed degree of kinship is exhausted, their tablets are transferred in succession. This accords with the principle in the “Royal Regulations” that the Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples, with the Zhou adding two perpetual shrines for Kings Wen and Wu. In winter and summer, sacrifices were formerly offered separately at…

translation_en:
…in the separate ancestral temples. Now, in the first month of spring, separate offerings preserve the honor due to all the temples; joint sacrifices in the other three seasons fulfill the rites of honoring a common ancestor. The great joint sacrifice in the last month of winter follows the institutions of Taizu’s own reign, while the year-end festival sacrifice is performed in Fengxian Hall. This embodies the principles set out in “Royal Regulations”: the Son of Heaven’s combined sacrifices designated here as jia-zhi, jia-di, jia-chang, and jia-zheng [?], together with the great joint sacrifice every three years. The rites have thus become still more exalted.
The great di sacrifice had formerly been omitted and left unperformed. Now sacrifice is offered retrospectively to the ancestor from whom Dezu descended, with Taizu associated with him in worship. An uninscribed spirit-seat is set up to receive the offerings. This both rejects the falsification of genealogical descent [?] and seeks sincerity within ourselves; it is especially sufficient to show that spiritual communion must occur. This embodies the ritual principle that only a king may perform the di sacrifice.

Now the great sacrifice to the Lord on High is performed in Xuanji Hall, with Ruizong associated with him in worship. Its timing in the last month of autumn draws upon the completion of the myriad precious products of the earth; the intention of honoring one’s father accords profoundly with the single source from which living things arise. title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:

作述以用中配古今而獨備是蓋
仁孝之至通于神明故

况今内外大小臣工未能盡承德意，禮樂之教發端於朝廷，而莫能宣布于天下。故品節限制之不相踰越，似亦可謂序矣，然驕亢者或至于欺凌，諂求者不謂其辱已；雍容揖讓之不相侵侮，似亦可謂和矣，然利害多出于面從，傾奪不下于讎敵。凡若此者，未必其盡去也。夫以如是諸臣，既不能以禮樂之道自淑其身心，又不能致禮樂之道以事乎君上，此亦教化、風俗、災害、生養四者之所由致也。
translation_en:
…the gentleman brings ritual to its fullest expression to regulate his person and music to its fullest expression to regulate his heart. Thus, if for even a moment he is neither solemn nor reverent, a spirit of carelessness and arrogance enters him; if for even a moment he is neither harmonious nor joyful, a spirit of baseness and deceit enters him.” Now, Your Majesty, from such minor matters as rising, retiring, eating, and resting to such major matters as punishments, rewards, and governmental actions, from moments spent alone deep within the palace to occasions of audience in the great court: does every single act indeed proceed entirely from centrality, rectitude, and harmony? In my ignorance, I do not understand what subjects are forbidden to speak of. I beg Your Majesty to spare me execution by the headsman's axe and to examine yourself. If all your acts accord with centrality, rectitude, and harmony, there will be little time to wait before governance and moral transformation flourish. If even one part in ten thousand fails to accord with them, this is indeed the root of rise and decline, deterioration and flourishing.

Moreover, officials great and small, both within the capital and outside it, are now unable fully to carry out your virtuous intentions. Instruction through ritual and music originates at court, yet no one can disseminate it throughout the realm. That distinctions of rank and prescribed limits are not transgressed might seem to qualify as order. Yet the arrogant sometimes go so far as to bully others, while those who seek advancement through flattery do not regard it as humiliating themselves [?]. That men bow and defer to one another with dignified ease, without encroachment or insult, might seem to qualify as harmony. Yet calculations of advantage and harm often arise beneath outward compliance, and their efforts to undermine and supplant one another are no less fierce than those of sworn enemies. Conduct of this sort has not necessarily been entirely eliminated. Officials such as these can neither improve their own persons and hearts through the Way of ritual and music nor bring that Way fully into practice in serving their sovereign. This too accounts for the conditions in the four areas of moral instruction, popular customs, disasters, and the people's livelihood and nurture.

If Your Majesty would truly heed your servant’s words and rouse yourself with vigorous resolve to rectify the court, thereby rectifying the hundred officials and the myriad people, then what you set forth would have a foundation and never be exhausted, while its implementation would proceed by stages without disorder. The results of supreme peace could then be achieved at once. How could Confucius’s words deceive us?

Yet your servant ventures to offer a further observation. Throughout the realm today, rites and music are employed in government. In sum, although practice cannot wholly accord with them, neither have they been entirely abandoned. Yet the means of promoting them and bringing about moral transformation through their influence truly originate in the schools, while the two classics of rites and music have long been fragmentary. An earlier writer said that their prescribed particulars can be set forth, but their meaning is difficult to understand. Even when those particulars survive, their meaning cannot be fully comprehended; how much more so when both particulars and meaning have been lost! The earlier Confucian scholar Zhu Xi once wished to take the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili) as the classic and the Record of Rites (Liji) as its commentary. For the Classic of Music, he proposed drawing upon Cai Yuanding’s New Book on the Pitch Pipes (Lülü Xinshu), together with separately investigating musical sounds to compile musical records [?].

Now we are fortunate to live at a time when Your Majesty wields the authority to establish rites and music. Surely among the great ministers there are some who could be entrusted with the task of editing and compiling these works? If these could indeed be distributed to the schools, the Confucian teachers brought together in their study, candidates selected through the examinations on this basis, and sufficient years allowed, then prolonged study and practice would surely bring forth people of ability. This, too, is a great undertaking in rites and music.

As for the foundation for establishing the supreme standard and the means of achieving good government, these lie solely in Your Majesty’s steadfast preservation of this mind: bringing the inner and outer into unity and maintaining the same orientation over both long and short periods. 臣潘晟。

臣對：臣聞，人君之治天下，必存諸中者有純王之心，而後達諸外者有純王之政。心與政通，而天下之化會于極矣。何謂政？禮樂通于天下，所以立風化之具者也。何謂心？和敬積於中涵，所以立禮樂之本者也。使和敬之極不脩于預養，則心有不純，而所以為制作之周者無其基；則雖禮樂之制，亦徒事為彌文，而政有不純，所以為推行之感者亦無其具。體用乖違，心迹馳悖，雖欲致天下於雍熈之化，其可得哉？故人君有志於禮樂者，亦惟致力於涵養，澄清其本源，使敬以直内、和以平中者，一復吾天德之良能，則中心清明，而無非僻之擾。然後以是發揮於禮樂，風動乎臣民，禮以導敬，樂以宣和，一本諸吾心之精蘊，則制用有本，而自無駁雜之偏。將見大禮一立，而天下之度以軌；大樂一宣，而天下之情以平。内外協一之妙，聖神功用之全，至此極矣。尚何教化風俗之不善、災害之不去、生養之不遂，有可言者乎？此唐虞三代由此其選，
translation_en:
Your servant Pan Sheng.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in governing All under Heaven, a ruler must first possess inwardly a heart of pure kingliness; only then can he manifest outwardly a government of pure kingliness. When heart and government communicate with one another, the moral transformation of All under Heaven reaches its highest standard. What is meant by government? Ritual and music extend throughout All under Heaven: they are the means by which moral influence and transformation are established. What is meant by the heart? Harmony and reverence accumulate and are nurtured within: they establish the foundation of ritual and music. If the utmost harmony and reverence are not cultivated through prior nurturing, the heart will lack purity, and the comprehensive establishment of institutions will have no foundation. Even the institutions of ritual and music will then amount merely to elaborate formalities. Government will lack purity, and there will likewise be no means of eliciting a response when these institutions are put into practice. With substance and function at odds, and the heart and outward conduct diverging, how could one bring All under Heaven to a state of harmonious and flourishing transformation, however much one wished to do so?

Thus, a ruler intent upon ritual and music must devote himself to inner cultivation and clarify their ultimate source. By making reverence straighten what is within and harmony bring balance to the inner heart, he must wholly recover the innate capacity of his Heaven-endowed virtue. His heart will then be clear and luminous, free from the disturbances of error and perversity. Only then should he express this through ritual and music, moving his officials and people as the wind moves things: ritual guiding them toward reverence, and music giving expression to harmony. When everything is rooted in the essential depths of his own heart, institutions and their application will have a foundation and will naturally be free from the distortions of mixed and impure elements. One will then see that, once the great rites are established, the standards of All under Heaven fall into their proper course; once the great music is sounded, the feelings of All under Heaven become balanced. The wondrous unity of inner and outer, and the full efficacy of sagely and spiritual power, reach their utmost perfection here. What grounds could then remain for speaking of deficiencies in moral instruction and customs, calamities that have not been dispelled, or failure to provide for the people's livelihood and nurture? It was through this that Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties attained their distinction [?]…

皇祖之所以創業
陛下之所以中興夫豈有二道哉欽惟
陛下以剛健中正之資懋正大光明之學觀聖賢
之格訓集帝王之大成制禮作樂一本之和
敬以為天下風今之臣民優柔浸漬諷詠涵
濡忘大化以出入者二十年于兹矣豈不盛
哉然猶不自滿假治不為治乃於
萬幾之暇特進臣等於
廷拳拳以禮樂之用未足以盡致天下之化者

陛下望道未見求治無已之盛心也第臣草茅疎
愚不足以仰承

translation_en:
…down to the means by which our imperial ancestor founded the dynasty and Your Majesty brought about its restoration—could there possibly be two different ways? I reverently consider how Your Majesty, endowed with strength, vigor, balance, and rectitude, diligently pursues upright and luminous learning, studies the exemplary teachings of sages and worthies, and brings together the great achievements of emperors and kings. In establishing ritual and creating music, you root both entirely in harmony and reverence, making them an example for all under Heaven. For twenty years now, officials and common people have been gently nurtured and steeped in these influences, reciting and chanting, imbibing their benefits, and going about their lives unconscious of this great transformation. Is this not magnificent? Yet you remain unsatisfied with yourself and do not regard the order achieved as sufficient. Amid your myriad affairs, you have specially summoned us to court and earnestly asked why the application of ritual and music has not yet sufficed to bring the transformation of all under Heaven to completion. This amply reveals Your Majesty’s noble resolve to seek the Way as though you had not yet glimpsed it, and to pursue good government without ceasing.
Yet I am an obscure, untutored, and ignorant man, unworthy to receive your gracious question. Nevertheless, “When the sovereign is truly a sage, his servants carry out his wishes without awaiting commands.” Having now personally witnessed the accomplishment of your moral transformation, and having received this further command from Your Majesty, how could I dare not reverently offer what I have learned throughout my life, to fulfill even a ten-thousandth part of your expectations? I have heard it said in the Classic: “Heaven is high and Earth is low; the myriad things are dispersed and distinct, and the institutions of ritual operate. title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
官也恭敬莊順禮之制也是禮樂之作本於
吾心者也又曰大禮必簡大樂必易禮至則
無怨樂至則不爭揖讓而治天下者禮樂之
謂也是禮樂之用通于天下者也故六經之
道雖帝王治天下之大經大法而其用之最
急本之所先尤有在于禮樂者誠如
聖制之所言矣然必原諸天地本諸吾心于是而
通之天下則無體之禮無聲之樂原於天理
之精微本諸吾心之性命初非聲容器數之
可拘者已先得于我是吾心之純固已備天
===
下之禮樂也由是以序天下即吾心之序推
之而制爲不易之禮則羣物知所以自別軌
于度而不能違由是以和天下即吾心之和
推之而制爲由衷之樂則百物知所以自化
協于和而不能拂非有所牽制強假於其間
也至德淵微之妙一理感通之機吾以出諸
性情者爲感天下豈有外於性情而得之也
哉故雖不齊以政而天下自無不正不糾以
刑而天下自不犯于刑又何必區區於品節
制度之間流宥刑辟之末乃能置天下以同

…are the functions of music; reverence, respect, dignity, and compliance are the forms of ritual.” Thus the creation of ritual and music is rooted in our own hearts. It also says: “Great ritual must be simple; great music must be easy. When ritual reaches perfection, there is no resentment; when music reaches perfection, there is no contention. To govern all under Heaven through bowing and yielding—this is what ritual and music mean.” Thus the workings of ritual and music extend throughout all under Heaven.

Although the Way of the Six Classics comprises the great guiding principles and laws by which emperors and kings govern all under Heaven, ritual and music hold a particular place as its most urgent application and foremost foundation. This is indeed as Your Majesty’s pronouncement states. Yet they must take their source from Heaven and Earth and their root in our own hearts, and only then be extended throughout the realm. Ritual without physical form and music without sound originate in the subtle essence of heavenly principle and are rooted in the nature and destiny endowed in our hearts. Never confined to sounds, appearances, implements, or prescribed numbers, they are already apprehended within oneself. Thus the purity of our hearts already contains the ritual and music of all under Heaven.

To bring order to the realm on this basis is to extend the order within our own hearts and establish it as unchanging ritual. All beings then know how to distinguish their proper places, conforming to the standards without departing from them. To bring harmony to the realm on this basis is to extend the harmony within our own hearts and establish it as music proceeding from within. All beings then know how to transform themselves, joining in harmony without opposing it. No constraint or forced contrivance intervenes. Such is the profound and subtle wonder of consummate virtue, the workings of the single principle through which influence and response pass. If I exert influence through what proceeds from my nature and feelings, how could anyone under Heaven receive it through anything outside their own nature and feelings?

Thus, even without regulation through governmental measures, everyone under Heaven will naturally be upright; without correction through punishments, no one will naturally incur punishment. Why, then, must one labor over the details of gradations, regulations, and institutions, or the subsidiary matters of exile, clemency, and penal sanctions, before one can bring the realm to a state of shared…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
亨同和之治乎不然聲色之於化民孔子何
鄙之爲末務不賞而民勸不怒而民威於鈇
鉞子思何必要於篤恭之盛乎此禮樂所以
爲出治之本而心之和敬則又禮樂之本也
嘗觀古之帝王矣典禮之惇咸韶之作堯舜
嘗以風乎唐虞矣而民之昭明協和者率本
其精一執中之㫖正德脩已之訓大夏大濩
之興禹湯嘗以振于夏商矣而民之脩和輯
寧者一本其祇德綏猷之精以至彛倫之叙
大武之作文武之重光相繼者亦以風乎周
===
室矣而民之時叙脩和者一出其徽柔懿恭
皇建有極之妙盖其和敬充積之餘既有純
王之心而禮樂四達之用又有純王之政故
其致教化之善大風俗之同九年七年之災
不爲盛治之累而引養引恬之樂自致兆民
之阜成也有由然矣夫何三代以降大道斯
湮叔孫綿蕞之儀武帝宗廟之樂漢若具其
文矣而嫚罵多慾則非積德之基房玄齡貞
觀之禮祖孝孫雅樂之定唐若有其儀矣而
慚德敗倫則非制用之本至于宋室之興立

…a government of shared prosperity and harmony? Otherwise, why would Confucius have disparaged sounds and appearances as merely secondary concerns in transforming the people? The people are encouraged without rewards and stand in greater awe than before executioners’ axes without any display of anger: why would Zisi have insisted that this depended upon the fullness of profound reverence? This is why rites and music are the foundation from which good government proceeds, while harmony and reverence within the heart are, in turn, the foundation of rites and music.

I have considered the sovereigns of antiquity. Through their earnest observance of prescribed rites and the creation of the Xian and Shao music, Yao and Shun exerted a transforming influence in the ages of Tang and Yu. Yet the people’s enlightenment and concord all rested upon their principle of refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to the mean. Through teachings on rectifying virtue and cultivating oneself [?], and the institution of the Great Xia and Great Huo music, Yu and Tang brought renewal to Xia and Shang. Yet the people’s cultivated harmony and settled peace rested wholly upon their consummate reverence for virtue and adherence to the proper way. Then came the ordering of the constant human relationships and the creation of the Great Wu music. Kings Wen and Wu, whose successive reigns shone with renewed brilliance, likewise exerted a transforming influence upon the Zhou house. Yet the people’s orderly relations and cultivated harmony arose entirely from the subtle efficacy of their gracious gentleness and admirable reverence, and of the sovereign’s establishment of the supreme standard. Their accumulated harmony and reverence gave them the hearts of true sage-kings; the operation of rites and music, reaching everywhere, gave them the government of true sage-kings as well. Thus there was a reason why they perfected moral instruction and broadly unified customs, why the disasters lasting nine and seven years did not mar their flourishing rule, and why the joy of enduring nurture and tranquillity naturally brought the myriad people to prosperity and fulfilment.

Why, then, after the Three Dynasties, was the Great Way obscured? With Shusun’s ceremonies rehearsed using cords and bundles of reeds, and Emperor Wu’s ancestral-temple music, the Han seemingly possessed the requisite forms. Yet insolent abuse and excessive desires could furnish no foundation for accumulated virtue. With Fang Xuanling’s rites of the Zhenguan era and Zu Xiaosun’s establishment of court music, the Tang seemingly possessed the requisite ceremonies. Yet shameful conduct and the corruption of human relationships could furnish no foundation for instituting these practices. As for the rise of the Song house and the founding…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
國雖云仁厚授禪亦非光明則禮雖定於聶
陳樂雖制於王竇要不過儀文器數之末而
已矣尚何望其秩天下以大序樂天下於太
和而使教化風俗之盡美災祥之盡去生養
之盡遂哉亦可慨也已故歐陽脩曰三代而
上治出于一而禮樂達于天下三代而下政
出于二而禮樂為虛名朱熹稱其為萬世不
易之定論豈不信哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸汛掃胡元舉衣冠於腥羶
振綱常於淪斁
===
登極肇政之初他務未恤而獨以禮樂為急大徵
天下名儒如曾魯徐一夔董彝梁寅之徒以
分麗諸局講究討論損益裁定禮觀會通之
繁而其數則有常吉禮十有四凶禮二軍禮
三賓禮二嘉禮五是也樂求聲氣之元而其
章則有九曰本太初仰大明民初生品物亨
御六龍泰階平君德成聖道成樂清寧是也
其他儀文器數周旋曲折載諸
大明集禮者已不假臣言而具昭矣然其所以能
於大亂之後不二十年而遂使教化孚於海

國雖云仁厚，授禪亦非光明，則禮雖定於聶陳，樂雖制於王竇，要不過儀文器數之末而已矣。尚何望其秩天下以大序，樂天下於太和，而使教化風俗之盡美、災祥之盡去、生養之盡遂哉？亦可慨也已！故歐陽脩曰：「三代而上，治出于一，而禮樂達于天下；三代而下，政出于二，而禮樂為虛名。」朱熹稱其為萬世不易之定論，豈不信哉？

洪惟我太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸，汛掃胡元，舉衣冠於腥羶，振綱常於淪斁。登極肇政之初，他務未恤，而獨以禮樂為急，大徵天下名儒，如曾魯、徐一夔、董彝、梁寅之徒，以分麗諸局，講究討論，損益裁定。禮觀會通之繁，而其數則有常：吉禮十有四，凶禮二，軍禮三，賓禮二，嘉禮五是也。樂求聲氣之元，而其章則有九，曰《本太初》、《仰大明》、《民初生》、《品物亨》、《御六龍》、《泰階平》、《君德成》、《聖道成》、《樂清寧》是也。其他儀文器數、周旋曲折，載諸《大明集禮》者，已不假臣言而具昭矣。然其所以能於大亂之後，不二十年，而遂使教化孚於海
translation_en:
…although the founding of the state was said to be humane and generous, its receipt of the throne through abdication was hardly aboveboard. Thus, although Nie and Chen established its rites, and Wang and Dou fashioned its music, these amounted merely to the peripheral details of ceremonial forms, ritual implements, and numerical prescriptions. How could one expect them to order All-under-Heaven through the great ordering principles, bring it joy in supreme harmony, perfect moral instruction and customs, eliminate all calamities and portents [?], and fully provide for the people’s livelihood and nurture? This is indeed lamentable! Thus Ouyang Xiu said: “From the Three Dynasties back into antiquity, governance issued from a single source, and rites and music reached throughout All-under-Heaven. After the Three Dynasties, government issued from two sources, and rites and music became empty names.” Zhu Xi called this a definitive judgment that would remain unchanged for ten thousand generations. Is it not indeed true?

We reverently reflect upon how our Emperor Taizu Gao rose like a dragon in the Huai region, swept away the barbarian Yuan, restored the caps and robes of civilized rule amid their rank and mutton-reeking ways, and revived the cardinal bonds and constant virtues from degradation. At the beginning of his reign, when he ascended the throne and inaugurated his government, he had yet to attend to other affairs but regarded rites and music alone as urgent. He broadly summoned the realm’s eminent Confucian scholars, such as Zeng Lu, Xu Yikui, Dong Yi, and Liang Yin, assigning them to the various bureaus to study, deliberate, remove or add provisions, and reach authoritative decisions. In rites, he surveyed the manifold practices and their interconnections, while their prescribed numbers were fixed: fourteen auspicious rites, two mourning rites, three military rites, two guest rites, and five celebratory rites. In music, he sought the origin of sound and vital energy; its compositions numbered nine: “Rooted in the Primordial Beginning,” “Looking Up to the Great Brilliance,” “When the People First Came into Being,” “The Myriad Things Flourish,” “Driving the Six Dragons,” “The Steps of Supreme Harmony Are Level,” “The Ruler’s Virtue Is Perfected,” “The Sagely Way Is Perfected,” and “Rejoicing in Clarity and Tranquility.” The remaining ceremonial forms, ritual implements, numerical prescriptions, and intricate movements recorded in the Collected Rites of the Great Ming are already fully manifest without requiring your servant’s explanation. Yet how was it that, within fewer than twenty years after great disorder, he could bring moral instruction to prevail as far as the sea…

隅，風俗還於淳厚，災害消於無虞，生養成於有象者，其故何哉？盖由我皇祖遠通天地之蘊，深知禮樂之源，有以啓之耳。臣伏觀，講《易》家人而知誠實威嚴之不可廢，則其致禮以治躬者，已與天地同其序；《祖訓》一書而叙君臣同遊之盛，則其致樂以治心者，已與天地同其和。其他如觀心之亭、精誠之錄、存心省躬之戒、導敬宣和之諭，雖難槩舉，要不外吾心之和敬以宣之也。此其所以致治之美，繼唐虞三代而陋漢唐宋於不居也歟？
然而時方草創，經綸間有未及；勢值初平，制作或有未周。而一時賛襄禮樂諸臣，如天地、禘嘗之典，祧廟、世室之儀，
translation_en:
…the farthest shores, customs returned to simplicity and sincerity, calamities vanished so that there was no cause for anxiety, and the people's nourishment and upbringing achieved manifest results—what explains this? It was because our imperial ancestor comprehended the profound mysteries of Heaven and Earth and understood deeply the source of rites and music, thereby providing the foundation for these achievements. Your servant has humbly observed that, in expounding the Family hexagram of the Book of Changes, he recognized that sincerity and dignified authority could not be dispensed with. Thus, in perfecting ritual to regulate his own conduct, he already shared the order of Heaven and Earth. The book Ancestral Injunctions recounts the flourishing fellowship of ruler and ministers taking their pleasure together. Thus, in perfecting music to regulate his heart, he already shared the harmony of Heaven and Earth. Other examples include the Pavilion for Contemplating the Heart, the Record of Utmost Sincerity, the admonition to preserve one's heart and examine one's conduct, and the instruction to foster reverence and spread harmony. Though these are difficult to enumerate comprehensively, their essential purpose was simply to give expression to the harmony and reverence within his own heart. Was this not why the excellence of his government continued that of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties, leaving the Han, Tang, and Song beneath comparison [?]?
Yet this was a time when the dynasty was first being founded, and some matters of government had not yet been attended to; peace had only just been established, and some institutions were perhaps not yet complete. Moreover, the ministers then assisting with rites and music, in such matters as the ceremonies for Heaven and Earth and the di and chang ancestral sacrifices, and the observances for ancestral temples whose tablets had been removed and for permanent ancestral shrines…

translation_en:
…and the rites of the great sacrifice in the Hall of Light: in these, too, they could not fully realize our sagely founder’s benevolent and filial intentions by restoring all the ancient institutions. When our successive sage sovereigns inherited the throne, they followed the established statutes. Their flourishing governance and transforming influence extended everywhere without interruption; yet, in matters of rites and music, they modestly deferred the task and had no opportunity to undertake it. Thus, the great expansion of these grand observances and the worthy advancement of the sagely plans, to bring the dynasty’s rites and music to full perfection, truly had to await the present day.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty possesses Heaven-endowed gifts and has established the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony. Your Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness grasps the secret of the transmission of the mind among emperors and kings; your annotations to the Five Admonitions reveal the essential workings of what Confucius transmitted and Yan Hui received. In your Record and Eulogy on Revering Heaven [?], your sagely reverence is one with Heaven and Earth; in your Poems on a Spring Outing [?], your sagely harmony shares the springtime renewal of all things. Thus, your continuation of the imperial ancestor’s glorious example, deepening the source of rites and music, has long been under way. You have now renewed the institutions, and their accomplishment presents a magnificent spectacle. Exercising your uniquely discerning imperial judgment and drawing widely upon excellent counsel, you have modeled your measures on what befits Heaven and Earth, followed the principles of yin and yang, weighed changes between antiquity and the present, and examined the proper ordering of the people and all things. You have fully expressed your benevolent and filial heart and embraced the institutions of emperors and kings.
At the beginning of your reign, you first produced the book Great Compendium on Clarifying Human Relations (Minglun dadian), rectifying names and examining their meanings, thereby establishing enduring norms. It is truly sufficient to refute a thousand…

translation_en:
…age-old errors that seem correct, and give enduring expression to the sage’s filial piety. As for rites that had not yet been fully restored to ancient practice, Your Majesty has revised and corrected them all. Heaven and Earth were formerly worshipped together, housed in the Hall of the Great Sacrifice. Now they are worshipped separately at the southern and northern suburban altars, embodying the principle of Heaven’s illumination and Earth’s discernment. Performing these rites on the two solstices expresses their grounding in yin and yang. Associating Emperor Taizu Gao with these sacrifices preserves exclusively his honor as founder of the dynasty.
Sacrifices in the ancestral temple formerly extended only to the four immediate ancestral generations, without reaching those from whom they descended. Now, in performing the great di sacrifice, worship is extended retrospectively to the ancestor from whom Dezu descended, with Taizu associated in the sacrifice. This accords with the ritual principle that only a king may perform the di sacrifice. As for the joint ancestral sacrifices, separate offerings are made in the first month of spring, and joint offerings in the other three seasons; a great joint sacrifice is held in the Imperial Ancestral Temple in the last month of winter, and a year-end seasonal sacrifice in the Hall for Ancestral Worship. These embody the principle of presenting seasonal offerings in spring and autumn. At the Sh ancestral temple (Shimiao), rites are performed only in the first month of each of the four seasons; at year’s end, the sacrifices return to…

translation_en:
…at Chongxian Hall, thus avoiding any intention of lavishing greater offerings on a close relative. In establishing the temples, the irreverence of housing the ancestors in a common hall was rejected, and the practice of setting up curtained enclosures was abolished. Taizu alone occupies the Imperial Ancestral Temple, properly enjoying the honor of facing south. Taizong’s temple became the Chengzu Temple, occupying the position above the three zhao positions. The six spirit tablets of Renzong, Xuanzong, and their successors each have a temple bearing its own designation. This follows the Zhou arrangement of seven ancestral temples with the addition of permanent temples for Kings Wen and Wu.
The Hall of Enlightenment had formerly been deficient in expressing affection for one’s kin. Now, in the final month of autumn, when all the precious products of the earth have ripened, a great sacrifice is offered to the Lord on High in Xuanji Hall, with Emperor Xian sharing the offering. This embodies the principle of venerating King Wen in the Hall of Enlightenment by having him share the sacrifice to the Lord on High. Other measures include correcting the improper choice of those who shared the offerings at the altars of Soil and Grain, rectifying the error of worshipping images of the First Sage, and establishing the music of the ancestral temples, setting forth its songs, and arranging its instruments and dances. All these measures adapt the precedents of the Three Dynasties and take the Offices of Zhou as their standard in reaching a settlement, thereby bringing the ritual institutions of this dynasty to full completion. 陛下乃曰復古禮樂以建中和之極朕之志也何
二十年間敎化未盡孚風俗未盡美災害未
盡殄生養未盡遂其故何與此固
陛下謙冲之志也然臣伏觀天下事勢亦未敢盡
以爲不然者蓋大化雖已行而江洋兆無故
之變蠻貊動不庭之征者未必盡其善良也
風俗雖大同而士民縱流蕩之趨中外競奢
punctuated:
仁人饗帝，孝子饗親之至誠，真足以考三王而不謬，俟後聖而不惑者也。豈非所以善繼皇祖欲爲之志，善述皇祖未成之事，而加以因時變遷之宜、與世推移之妙哉？天下臣民樂聖人之有作，覩禮樂之大成，鼓舞作興，盖已不待刑政之驅馳，而會歸于典禮，不敢越度以自敗；樂化於和平，而不敢縱欲以傷生，宜可以爲中興之慶矣。
而陛下乃曰：「復古禮樂，以建中和之極，朕之志也。何二十年間，教化未盡孚，風俗未盡美，災害未盡殄，生養未盡遂，其故何與？」此固陛下謙冲之志也。然臣伏觀天下事勢，亦未敢盡以爲不然者。盖大化雖已行，而江洋兆無故之變，蠻貊動不庭之征者，未必盡其善良也。風俗雖大同，而士民縱流蕩之趨，中外競奢
translation_en:
…the utmost sincerity with which a humane man offers sacrifice to the Lord on High and a filial son offers sacrifice to his parents truly stands comparison with the Three Kings without error and can await a sage of later ages without misgiving. Is this not how Your Majesty has worthily carried forward the intentions of your imperial ancestor and worthily continued the undertakings that your imperial ancestor left unfinished, adding the fitting adaptations required by changing times and the subtle skill of keeping pace with the age? All the officials and people under Heaven rejoice in the sage’s achievements and behold the great perfection of rites and music. Inspired and stirred to action, they surely no longer need the driving force of punishments and government to bring them together in observance of ritual institutions, nor do they dare transgress the prescribed bounds and bring ruin upon themselves. Gladly transformed toward peace and harmony, they dare not indulge desires that would harm their lives. This should indeed be cause to celebrate a dynastic resurgence.
Yet Your Majesty has said: “To restore the rites and music of antiquity and thereby establish the highest standard of equilibrium and harmony is my aspiration. Why, over these twenty years, has moral instruction not yet won complete trust, have customs not yet become wholly good, have calamities not yet been wholly eliminated, and have the people’s livelihoods and nurture not yet been fully secured? What is the reason?” This certainly expresses Your Majesty’s humility. Yet, respectfully observing the state of affairs under Heaven, your servant does not dare deem these concerns wholly unfounded. For although your great transforming influence has already spread, unprovoked disturbances are brewing on the rivers and seas, while the Man and Mo peoples provoke punitive expeditions by failing to submit to court. Thus, not all have become good and law-abiding. Although customs have largely become uniform, scholars and commoners give free rein to dissipation, and those within and beyond the capital vie in extravagance…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
麗之尚者未必盡其儉飭也災害雖天心所
以仁愛而頻年風霾之迭見水旱之繼仍終
非善政之感也生養雖王政得以安遂而窮
民苦於征役富室困於貪漁要皆惠德之虧
也是四者之未盡
陛下因之以自慊臣不佞謂
陛下雖居
九重之邃而明見萬里之外有如是也雖或百姓
之愚未必由通於孝弟而日用之知故無以
與能於禮樂有以致之耳臣切意帝舜之聖
===

迪哲之餘或者
陛下盛德雖云無瑕中和雖建有極而心神感運
之下猶未盡入於淵微之域而綏來動和之
妙乃未得於和敬之薫蒸此四者之累所以
不能不厪
陛下之憂也而復求禮樂刑政四達不悖之道以
比隆于先王之盛臣非有知者而何以對揚
乎然亦有說焉臣聞天下之道無間于隱微
而人君之德常存於戒懼苟執禮者矜持于

…a taste for splendor, they may not all be frugal and disciplined. Although calamities are Heaven’s means of expressing benevolent concern, the repeated appearance of windstorms and dust haze year after year, and the succession of floods and droughts, are ultimately no response to good government. Although royal government enables people to live and sustain themselves in peace, the poor suffer from levies and labor service, while wealthy households are distressed by greedy exactions. These are all, in essence, deficiencies in beneficent virtue. Because these four matters remain unfulfilled, Your Majesty finds cause for dissatisfaction with yourself. Your untalented servant considers that, although Your Majesty dwells deep within the ninefold palace, you see affairs ten thousand li away with just such clarity. Perhaps the common people, in their ignorance, do not fully comprehend filial devotion and brotherly respect, and their everyday understanding therefore does not enable them to participate capably in rites and music [?]; there must be something that has brought this about.
Your servant humbly reflects that even Emperor Shun, with all his sageliness, transformed the Miao only after withdrawing his troops; and the Three Ancestral Sovereigns, with all their virtue, reproached themselves for their faults even after attaining wisdom. Perhaps, although Your Majesty’s abundant virtue may be called flawless, and you have established the highest standard of equilibrium and harmony, the responsive workings of your mind and spirit have yet to penetrate fully into the profound and subtle realm. Perhaps the wondrous efficacy of bringing peace so that people come willingly, and stirring them so that they become harmonious, has yet to emerge from the pervasive influence of harmony and reverence. These burdens in the four matters therefore cannot but trouble Your Majesty. You further seek the Way by which rites, music, punishments, and government operate everywhere without conflict, so as to match the flourishing achievements of the former kings. Your servant is no man of understanding: how could I respond worthily to your command? Yet there is something I can offer. Your servant has heard that the Way of the world leaves no gap even in what is hidden and subtle, and that a ruler’s virtue always rests in vigilance and apprehension. If one who administers rites maintains a punctilious demeanor in…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
儀文制度之間而宴閒之或褻則即此空隙
之中而慢易之心已入雖欲責天下以同禮
其如中心之不敬何哉治樂者矯飾於聲音
蹈舞之際而侈欲之或愆則即此淫放之內
而鄙詐之念已萌雖欲强天下以同樂其如
中心之不和何哉此其為功愈難而致效亦
愈遠也臣伏願
陛下致禮以治躬不惟
宗廟
朝廷雖
===
深宮內寢侍御僕從亦必如大祭之承大賓之
接而不敢有一息之懈以肆於內致樂以治
心不惟聲依律和雖一事一物一言一動亦
必如大羹之調大鼎之烹而不敢有一毫之
過以流於淫則功深於顧諟力積於潛微
陛下所以行於
郊社禘嘗者不徒蒼璧黃琮之陳而
仁人誠敬之心自可以通徹于天下不惟秉璧植
圭之具而
孝子信慤之念自可以感動於萬方故雖不必道

punctuated:
儀文制度之間，而宴閒之或褻，則即此空隙之中，而慢易之心已入。雖欲責天下以同禮，其如中心之不敬何哉？治樂者矯飾於聲音蹈舞之際，而侈欲之或愆，則即此淫放之內，而鄙詐之念已萌。雖欲强天下以同樂，其如中心之不和何哉？此其為功愈難，而致效亦愈遠也。
臣伏願陛下致禮以治躬，不惟宗廟、朝廷，雖深宮內寢、侍御僕從，亦必如大祭之承、大賓之接，而不敢有一息之懈以肆於內；致樂以治心，不惟聲依律和，雖一事一物、一言一動，亦必如大羹之調、大鼎之烹，而不敢有一毫之過以流於淫。則功深於顧諟，力積於潛微。陛下所以行於郊社禘嘗者，不徒蒼璧黃琮之陳，而仁人誠敬之心自可以通徹于天下；不惟秉璧植圭之具，而孝子信慤之念自可以感動於萬方。故雖不必道
translation_en:
… amid ceremonial forms and institutions, yet sometimes lapse into irreverence in private leisure, then through this very opening a careless and disrespectful disposition has already entered. Even if one wishes to require all under Heaven to conform to the same rites, what can be done about the lack of reverence within one’s own heart? Those who regulate music may affect correctness in sounds and dance movements, yet sometimes err through extravagant desires; within this very indulgence, base and deceitful thoughts have already sprouted. Even if they wish to compel all under Heaven to share the same music, what can be done about the lack of harmony within their own hearts? This makes the work ever more difficult and its results ever more remote.
Your servant humbly wishes that Your Majesty would bring ritual propriety to perfection to govern your person. Not only in the ancestral temple and at court, but even in the secluded palace and inner sleeping chambers, and in dealing with attendants and servants, you should invariably act as though conducting a great sacrifice or receiving an honored guest, never daring to relax for a single moment and become unrestrained in private. Bring music to perfection to govern your heart. Not only should its sounds accord harmoniously with the pitch standards: in every affair and every thing, every word and every movement, you should act as though preparing the great sacrificial broth or cooking in the great cauldron, never daring to exceed the proper measure in the slightest and lapse into excess. Then your achievement in keeping virtue constantly in view will deepen, and your efforts will accumulate in the hidden and subtle recesses of the heart.
What Your Majesty performs in the suburban sacrifices to Heaven, the sacrifices to the soil, and the di and chang ancestral sacrifices will then be more than a display of azure jade disks and yellow jade tubes: the sincere and reverent heart of a benevolent person will of itself reach throughout all under Heaven. It will be more than the ceremonial formalities of holding jade disks and setting upright jade tablets: the faithful and earnest thoughts of a filial son will of themselves move all regions. Thus, even without necessarily guiding them …

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
之以政齊之以刑而君臣篤於義父子厚於
親長幼明於序内外嚴於別天下之會歸於
禮者固不戒而孚之矣暴民不作諸侯賓服
兵革不試五刑不用百姓無怨而天下之和
平于樂者自不行而至之矣如此則教化不
必推而道德自是丕冒也風俗不必同而廉
恥自是其重也災害不必消而太和已積自
致禎祥之兆生養不求遂而居業有常自享
利樂之成孔子所謂言而履之禮也行而樂
之樂也力此二者南面而立是以天下太平
===
不於是而益可信耶雖然其要猶有不在於
是也臣聞程頤曰明君以務學為急聖學以
正心為要真德秀曰惟敬可以存此心惟學
可以養此心惟親近賢人君子可以維持此
心即二言觀之人君進德脩業尤莫有過於
學者矣苟有和敬之心而無學問之力臣恐
不淪於虛無而無實用之妙則涉於利欲而
多戕賊之非日轉月移之間其有存焉者亦
寡矣
陛下誠欲和敬之心常存無斁則必於

寡矣
陛下誠欲和敬之心常存無斁則必於
punctuated:
之以政，齊之以刑，而君臣篤於義，父子厚於親，長幼明於序，内外嚴於別，天下之會歸於禮者，固不戒而孚之矣。暴民不作，諸侯賓服，兵革不試，五刑不用，百姓無怨，而天下之和平于樂者，自不行而至之矣。如此，則教化不必推，而道德自是丕冒也；風俗不必同，而廉恥自是其重也；災害不必消，而太和已積，自致禎祥之兆；生養不求遂，而居業有常，自享利樂之成。孔子所謂「言而履之，禮也；行而樂之，樂也。力此二者，南面而立，是以天下太平」，不於是而益可信耶？
雖然，其要猶有不在於是也。臣聞程頤曰：「明君以務學為急，聖學以正心為要。」真德秀曰：「惟敬可以存此心，惟學可以養此心，惟親近賢人君子可以維持此心。」即二言觀之，人君進德脩業，尤莫有過於學者矣。苟有和敬之心，而無學問之力，臣恐不淪於虛無而無實用之妙，則涉於利欲而多戕賊之非。日轉月移之間，其有存焉者亦寡矣。陛下誠欲和敬之心常存無斁，則必於
translation_en:
…guide them through government and regulate them through punishments, yet rulers and ministers will be steadfast in righteousness, fathers and sons deeply affectionate, elders and juniors clear about their proper order, and those within and without strict in observing their distinctions. All under Heaven will assuredly come together in ritual propriety, trusting in it without being admonished. Violent people will not rise up, the regional lords will submit as guests, arms will not be put to use, the five punishments will not be applied, and the common people will have no grievances. The peace and harmony of all under Heaven expressed in music will arrive of themselves, without being deliberately brought about. Thus moral instruction need not be extended, for the Way and virtue will themselves spread everywhere; customs need not be made uniform, for integrity and a sense of shame will themselves be esteemed. Disasters need not be dispelled: supreme harmony, already accumulated, will naturally bring auspicious signs. There will be no need to seek the fulfillment of the people's livelihood and nurture: with settled dwellings and occupations, they will naturally enjoy the fruits of prosperity and contentment. Confucius said: “To speak and put one's words into practice is ritual propriety; to act and take joy in it is music. Exert oneself in these two, and stand facing south as ruler: thereby all under Heaven is at peace.” Does this not make his words still more worthy of belief?
Even so, there remains an essential point that lies elsewhere. Your servant has heard Cheng Yi say: “An enlightened ruler regards diligent learning as urgent; the learning of the sages regards rectifying the mind as essential.” Zhen Dexiu said: “Only reverence can preserve this mind; only learning can nourish this mind; only drawing close to worthy men and gentlemen can sustain this mind.” Judging from these two statements, nothing surpasses learning in enabling a ruler to advance his virtue and cultivate his endeavors. If he possesses a harmonious and reverent mind but lacks the strength supplied by learning, your servant fears that he will either sink into emptiness and nothingness, lacking the subtle efficacy of practical application, or become entangled in profit and desire, committing many wrongs that injure his mind. As days turn and months pass, little of it will remain. If Your Majesty truly wishes to preserve a harmonious and reverent mind constantly, without weariness, then you must, in…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
萬幾之暇爰稽古典以求二帝三王所以傳心之
要道親賢人厚君子以為學問自脩之培植
經筵
御講必求其明善誠身之要而不徒于文章句誦
之煩諫臺
受言必取其涵養身心之助而不徒于用人行政
之末則出諸人者實所以裕於已而受諸已
者皆所以自養其學也他如師巫足以淫此
學者辨之而不信土木足以荒此學者阻之
而不興聲色足以蕩此學者屏之而不邇貨
===
利足以卑此學者賤之而不殖則外物之干
不擾而純王之心自在豈不足以常存和敬
出純王之政而為鼓舞天下之機哉伊尹之
告太甲曰德無常師主善為師正取人為學
之要也傅說之告高宗曰念終始典于學厥
德脩罔覺正恒以敏學之功也臣草茅愚士
雖不敢上擬伊傅而平生致
君之心亦自知以二臣為慕也故篇終敢附二臣
之言以為
陛下盛德加勉之少助焉伏惟

德脩罔覺正恒以敬學之功也〔臣草茅愚士〕
雖不敢上擬伊傳而平生致
君之心亦自知以二臣爲慕也故篇終敢附二臣
之言以爲
陛下盛德加勉之少助焉伏惟
punctuated:
萬幾之暇，爰稽古典，以求二帝三王所以傳心之要道；親賢人，厚君子，以為學問自脩之培植。經筵御講，必求其明善誠身之要，而不徒于文章句誦之煩；諫臺受言，必取其涵養身心之助，而不徒于用人行政之末。則出諸人者，實所以裕於已，而受諸已者，皆所以自養其學也。他如師巫足以淫此學者，辨之而不信；土木足以荒此學者，阻之而不興；聲色足以蕩此學者，屏之而不邇；貨利足以卑此學者，賤之而不殖。則外物之干不擾，而純王之心自在，豈不足以常存和敬，出純王之政，而為鼓舞天下之機哉！
伊尹之告太甲曰：「德無常師，主善為師。」正取人為學之要也。傅說之告高宗曰：「念終始典于學，厥德脩罔覺。」正恒以敏學之功也。臣草茅愚士，雖不敢上擬伊傅，而平生致君之心，亦自知以二臣為慕也。故篇終敢附二臣之言，以為陛下盛德加勉之少助焉。伏惟
translation_en:
…in the leisure afforded by the myriad affairs of state, consult the ancient canons to seek the essential Way by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings transmitted their understanding of the heart. Draw worthy men close and treat gentlemen generously, thereby nurturing learning and self-cultivation. In the lectures delivered before Your Majesty at the Classics Colloquium, seek above all the essentials of understanding goodness and making oneself sincere, rather than merely dwelling on the intricacies of literary composition and the recitation of passages. In receiving counsel from remonstrating officials, take from it whatever helps nurture body and mind, rather than attending merely to such subsidiary matters as employing personnel and administering government. Then what comes from others will truly enrich oneself, and everything one receives will nourish one’s own learning. As for spirit mediums whose practices might lead this learning astray, discern their falsity and do not believe them. As for construction projects that might cause this learning to be neglected, restrain them and do not undertake them. As for music and sensual pleasures that might unsettle this learning, banish them and do not approach them. As for wealth and profit that might debase this learning, disdain them and do not accumulate them. Then the intrusion of external things will cause no disturbance, and the heart of pure kingly rule will remain intact of itself. Would this not suffice to preserve harmony and reverence constantly, bring forth the government of pure kingly rule, and provide the means to inspire all under Heaven?
Yi Yin admonished Tai Jia: “In virtue there is no fixed teacher; take goodness as your teacher.” This precisely expresses the essential principle of learning from others. Fu Yue admonished Gaozong: “Keep learning constantly in mind, from beginning to end, and your virtue will develop without your noticing it.” This precisely expresses the achievement of persevering in diligent learning. Your servant is a foolish scholar from the countryside. Although I dare not compare myself with Yi Yin and Fu Yue above me, I know that, in my lifelong desire to guide my ruler toward perfection, I have taken these two ministers as my models. Thus, at the end of this essay, I venture to append their words, as a small aid to Your Majesty’s further cultivation of your abundant virtue. I humbly hope…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
陛下矜其愚不錄其罪擇之千慮而取其一得則
天下幸甚愚臣幸甚臣干瀆
天威不勝恐懼隕越之至臣謹對

天下幸甚愚臣幸甚臣干瀆
天威不勝恐懼隕越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 陛下矜其愚，不錄其罪，擇之千慮而取其一得，則天下幸甚，愚臣幸甚！臣干瀆天威，不勝恐懼隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …may Your Majesty pity my ignorance, refrain from recording my offense, and select from my thousand deliberations the one sound thought. Then the realm would be most fortunate, and your foolish servant most fortunate! Having presumed to offend Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring authority, your servant is overwhelmed by fear and dread, as if about to fall. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
臣林一鳳
臣對臣聞人君有純天之心者而後可以語
憲天之道有憲天之道者而後可以語格天
之功心者治之本也道者治之迹也道本乎
心則動之有幾作之有自由是而一則天天
則神治本於道則推無不準動無不化由是
而明則章章則溥故曰天下之治本于道天
下之道本于心否則有其心而不能達于道
者是謂徒善徒善不足以為政竊夫道而不
統于心者是謂徒法徒法不能以自行要之
===
功皆小補而能有成夫格天之治者臣未之
前聞也是故中和也者純天之心也禮樂也
者憲天之道也化行俗美政治民安者格天
之功也此固堯舜禹湯文武聖人之能事而
我
國家之所以比隆唐虞三代者率惟此道而已
彼三代而下之君果有一於是乎欽惟
皇帝陛下稟神聖之資際文明之運有內聖外王
之學有通變宜民之政居仁秉智而無體不
遺思艱圖易而憂勤靡懈篤於欽

punctuated:
臣林一鳳。
臣對：臣聞人君有純天之心者，而後可以語憲天之道；有憲天之道者，而後可以語格天之功。心者，治之本也；道者，治之迹也。道本乎心，則動之有幾，作之有自，由是而一則天，天則神。治本於道，則推無不準，動無不化，由是而明則章，章則溥。故曰：天下之治本于道，天下之道本于心。否則，有其心而不能達于道者，是謂徒善，徒善不足以為政；竊夫道而不統于心者，是謂徒法，徒法不能以自行。要之，功皆小補，而能有成夫格天之治者，臣未之前聞也。是故中和也者，純天之心也；禮樂也者，憲天之道也；化行俗美、政治民安者，格天之功也。此固堯舜禹湯文武聖人之能事，而我國家之所以比隆唐虞三代者，率惟此道而已。彼三代而下之君，果有一於是乎？欽惟皇帝陛下，稟神聖之資，際文明之運，有內聖外王之學，有通變宜民之政，居仁秉智而無體不遺，思艱圖易而憂勤靡懈，篤於欽
translation_en:
Your servant, Lin Yifeng.
Your servant replies: I have heard that only when a ruler possesses a heart wholly aligned with Heaven can one speak of his way of modeling himself upon Heaven; only when he possesses that way can one speak of his achievement in reaching Heaven. The heart is the root of government; the Way is government’s outward manifestation. When the Way is rooted in the heart, every movement has its incipient impulse and every undertaking its source. Thus, unity leads to accord with Heaven, and accord with Heaven leads to spiritual efficacy. When government is rooted in the Way, every application accords with the standard, and every action brings transformation. Thus, illumination leads to manifest brilliance, and manifest brilliance to all-pervading influence. Hence it is said: government throughout the world is rooted in the Way, and the Way throughout the world is rooted in the heart. Otherwise, possessing such a heart but being unable to realize it in the Way is called mere goodness; mere goodness is insufficient for governing. Appropriating the Way without unifying it in the heart is called mere law; mere law cannot carry itself into effect. Ultimately, the achievements of either amount only to minor improvements. I have never heard of anyone thereby accomplishing government that reaches Heaven.
Thus, equilibrium and harmony constitute the heart wholly aligned with Heaven; rites and music constitute the way of modeling oneself upon Heaven; and the spread of moral transformation, the refinement of customs, orderly government, and a peaceful populace constitute the achievement of reaching Heaven. These were indeed the accomplishments of the sages Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. It is solely by following this Way that our dynasty has equaled the flourishing rule of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Did any ruler after the Three Dynasties truly possess even one of these qualities?
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with spiritual sagacity and has encountered an age of cultural brilliance. You possess the learning of inward sagehood and outward kingship, and your government adapts to changing circumstances for the people’s benefit. You abide in benevolence and uphold wisdom, leaving no aspect unembodied [?]; you ponder difficulties and plan for ease, never slackening in care and diligence, steadfast in reverence …

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
天法
祖誠於尚德緩刑自
即位以来凡六策士于兹首之以因革之宜則通
變宜民之政也繼之以王伯之辨則内聖外
王之學也次三則有知人安民之詢是欲兼
體夫仁智矣次四則有足民衣食之問是欲
思艱而圖易矣次五曰創守匹休則敬
天法
祖之意昭矣次六曰仁義並用則尚德緩刑之情
見矣廼
今二十年于兹
中和建極禮樂明備化行而俗美政久而民安
雖唐虞三代之世不能過矣方且
謙冲自居望道未見復進臣等於
廷降賜
清問而及禮樂之事顧臣草莽疎賤豈能達禮樂
之本識禮樂之情者然竊願學焉而未能也
敢不掇拾所聞以對揚
休命之萬一乎臣聞天高地下萬物散殊而禮興
矣流而不息合同而化而樂行焉是禮非無

===
今二十年于茲
中和建極禮樂明備化行而俗美政乂而民安
雖唐虞三代之世不能過矣方且
謙冲自居望道未見復進臣等於
廷降賜
清問而及禮樂之事顧臣草莽疎賤豈能達禮樂
之本識禮樂之情者然竊願學焉而未能也
敢不掇拾所聞以對揚
休命之萬一乎臣聞天高地下萬物散殊而禮興
矣流而不息合同而化而樂行焉是禮非無
punctuated:
天法祖，誠於尚德緩刑。自即位以来，凡六策士于兹：首之以因革之宜，則通變宜民之政也；繼之以王伯之辨，則内聖外王之學也；次三則有知人安民之詢，是欲兼體夫仁智矣；次四則有足民衣食之問，是欲思艱而圖易矣；次五曰創守匹休，則敬天法祖之意昭矣；次六曰仁義並用，則尚德緩刑之情見矣。廼今二十年于兹，中和建極，禮樂明備，化行而俗美，政久而民安，雖唐虞三代之世不能過矣。方且謙冲自居，望道未見，復進臣等於廷，降賜清問，而及禮樂之事。顧臣草莽疎賤，豈能達禮樂之本、識禮樂之情者？然竊願學焉而未能也，敢不掇拾所聞，以對揚休命之萬一乎？

臣聞天高地下，萬物散殊，而禮興矣；流而不息，合同而化，而樂行焉。是禮非無
translation_en:
…Heaven and emulating your ancestors, and sincere in honoring virtue and tempering punishments. Since ascending the throne, you have on six occasions examined scholars with policy questions. The first concerned what should be retained and what changed: this was government that adapts to changing circumstances for the people's benefit. The next concerned the distinction between kingly and hegemonic rule: this was the learning of inward sagehood and outward kingship. The third asked about understanding men and bringing peace to the people: this expressed your desire to embody both benevolence and wisdom. The fourth asked about providing the people with sufficient clothing and food: this expressed your desire to consider difficulties and devise ways to ease them. The fifth spoke of founding and maintaining a dynasty as equally glorious: this made manifest your intention to revere Heaven and emulate your ancestors. The sixth spoke of employing benevolence and righteousness together: this revealed your commitment to honoring virtue and tempering punishments. Now, twenty years into your reign, you have established the supreme standard through equilibrium and harmony; rites and music are clearly ordered and fully developed. Your transforming influence has spread and customs have become good; your government has endured and the people are at peace. Even the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties could not surpass this. Yet you continue to comport yourself with humility, seeking the Way as though you had not yet perceived it. Once again, you have summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your august questions, addressing the affairs of rites and music. But I, your servant, am an obscure and lowly man from the countryside: how could I comprehend the foundations of rites and music or understand their essential character? Nevertheless, I privately aspire to learn these things, though I have not yet succeeded. Dare I fail to gather what I have heard, so as to respond to and extol even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command?

Your servant has heard that Heaven is high and Earth is low, and the myriad things are dispersed and distinct: thus ritual arises. They flow without ceasing, unite, and undergo transformation: thus music operates. Hence ritual is not without …

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
因而強作也法天地自然之序為之也樂非
作而致其情也法天地自然之和為之也稽
諸古昔唐虞命伯夷典禮命后夔典樂而黎
民於變四方風動之化成夏商周有典有則
經禮曲禮之制大夏大濩大武之作而兆民
阜成四海永清之治致然要之此其經綸之
迹耳而制作之本固有在也是故堯之峻德
舜之重華禹湯之建中建極文武之敬止敬
勝其中和之本已具矣則夫出於朝廷而行
於郊廟用之鄉人而達於邦國後有作者斯
===
其不可及乎故歐陽脩曰三代而上治出于
一而禮樂達于天下此也厥後叔孫綿蕞之
儀開元慶曆之制後世之所謂禮也而君子
非之安世房中之歌七德廟中之舞後世之
所謂樂也而識者鄙之然要之竊其聲容之
末耳而制作之本固未聞也是故馬上之習
未去而擊劔之風尚存閨中之德以慚而舞
干之儀何在其中和之極已亡矣則其著于
籩豆簠簋與夫升降揖遜形于干戚羽旄與
夫清濁長短者末節可觀亦奚足貴哉故歐

其不可及乎故歐陽脩曰三代而上治出于
一而禮樂達于天下此也厥後叔孫綿蕞之
儀開元慶曆之制後世之所謂禮也而君子
非之安世房中之歌七德廟中之舞後世之
所謂樂也而識者鄙之然要之竊其聲容之
末耳而制作之本固未聞也是故馬上之習
未去而擊鞠之風尚存閨中之德以慚而舞
干之儀何在其中和之極已亡矣則其著于
籩豆簠簋與夫升降揖遜形于干戚羽旄與
夫清濁長短者未節可觀亦奚足貴哉故歐
punctuated:
因而強作也，法天地自然之序為之也。樂非作而致其情也，法天地自然之和為之也。稽諸古昔，唐虞命伯夷典禮，命后夔典樂，而黎民於變、四方風動之化成。夏商周有典有則，經禮曲禮之制，《大夏》《大濩》《大武》之作，而兆民阜成、四海永清之治致。然要之，此其經綸之迹耳，而制作之本固有在也。是故堯之峻德，舜之重華，禹湯之建中建極，文武之敬止敬勝，其中和之本已具矣。則夫出於朝廷而行於郊廟，用之鄉人而達於邦國，後有作者，斯其不可及乎？
故歐陽脩曰：「三代而上，治出于一，而禮樂達于天下。」此也。厥後叔孫綿蕞之儀，開元慶曆之制，後世之所謂禮也，而君子非之；安世房中之歌，七德廟中之舞，後世之所謂樂也，而識者鄙之。然要之，竊其聲容之末耳，而制作之本固未聞也。是故馬上之習未去，而擊劔之風尚存；閨中之德以慚，而舞干之儀何在？其中和之極已亡矣。則其著于籩豆簠簋與夫升降揖遜，形于干戚羽旄與夫清濁長短者，末節可觀，亦奚足貴哉？故歐
translation_en:
…arbitrarily contrived without a basis; rather, ritual was fashioned on the natural order of Heaven and Earth. Music likewise does not bring its feelings into being through contrivance; it is fashioned on the natural harmony of Heaven and Earth. Looking back to antiquity, in the ages of Tang and Yu, Bo Yi was commanded to oversee ritual and Hou Kui to oversee music. Thus the transforming influence that changed the common people and stirred the four quarters like the wind was accomplished. The Xia, Shang, and Zhou had their statutes and standards, their institutions of fundamental ritual and detailed observances, and their compositions Great Xia, Great Hu, and Great Wu. Thus they achieved government under which the myriad people prospered and the lands within the four seas enjoyed lasting peace. Yet these were, in essence, merely the outward traces of their ordering of the world; the foundation of their institutions and compositions lay elsewhere. Thus Yao’s lofty virtue, Shun’s successive brilliance, Yu’s and Tang’s establishment of the mean and the supreme standard, and Wen’s and Wu’s abiding in reverence and prevailing through reverence already embodied the foundation of equilibrium and harmony. What then issued from the court and was practiced at the suburban altars and ancestral temples, employed among village people and extended throughout the states—could later creators ever equal it?
Hence Ouyang Xiu said, “Under the Three Dynasties and earlier, government issued from a single source, and ritual and music reached throughout the world.” This is what he meant. Thereafter came Shusun’s ceremonies rehearsed with bundles of reeds marking the positions, and the institutions of the Kaiyuan and Qingli eras: these were what later ages called ritual, yet gentlemen condemned them. The Songs for Pacifying the Age performed in the inner chambers and the Dance of the Seven Virtues performed in the ancestral temple were what later ages called music, yet discerning men disdained them. In essence, they merely appropriated the superficial details of sound and ceremonial appearance; of the foundation for creating such institutions they had heard nothing. Thus the habits of horseback rule had not been cast off, and the custom of swordplay still remained. Virtue within the women’s quarters gave cause for shame; where, then, was the proper bearing for the shield dance? The supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony had already been lost. What found expression in bamboo offering baskets, stemmed dishes, and square and round grain vessels, together with ascending and descending, bowing and yielding precedence; and what took form in shields and axes, feathers and yak-tail pennons, together with high and low pitches and long and short notes—these minor details might be worth watching, but what made them worthy of esteem? Hence Ou…

title: 嘉靖二十年進士登科錄
text:
陽脩曰三代而下治出于二而禮樂徒為虛
文此也盖禮樂者為治之道也而六經所陳
亦不能外此以為之用如書之命夷命夔易
之定志殷薦春秋之兩觀六羽何者而不相
通于道耶然則漢史所謂六經之道同歸而
禮樂之用為急者義固有所偏也禮樂者為
治之本也而政刑所在亦惟輔其治之所不
及如唐虞士師之官商人官刑之儆成周司
寇之屬是豈盛世之所偏廢哉然則
聖制所謂政刑末務果不足以為治者意固有所
===
===
在也洪惟
太祖高皇帝獨稟全智超越千古明華夏于既污
復衣冠于左衽乃于
